triage.name: Fainting
triage.reason: Syncope is a classic undifferentiated symptom with a broad differential (cardiac, reflex, orthostatic) reachable by history, orthostatics, ECG and targeted testing.

age.peak: bimodal: teens/young adults and adults over 60

demographics: Reflex (vasovagal) fainting is the most common type and is especially frequent in adolescents and young adults
Fainting from heart rhythm problems or orthostatic causes becomes more common with age
Lifetime occurrence is common in the general population

risk_factors.text: Prolonged standing, warm environments, or crowded rooms
Emotional stress, pain, or the sight of blood

comorbidities: Heart disease, including arrhythmias, valve disease, or heart failure
Parkinson disease or other conditions causing autonomic dysfunction
family_history: Fainting or sudden cardiac death in a close relative
social_history: Athletic training or military drill with prolonged standing

chief_complaints.text: I felt like I was going to faint
I blacked out for a few seconds

hpi.onset: Sudden, often while standing or shortly after standing up
hpi.duration: Loss of consciousness lasts seconds to about a minute; full recovery within minutes
hpi.progression: A warning feeling of lightheadedness, warmth, or nausea builds over seconds, then consciousness is lost and the person slumps or falls; recovery is quick and complete
hpi.quality: Brief loss of consciousness with loss of muscle tone
hpi.severity: Episodes are brief but can cause injury from falling
hpi.timing: Occurs while standing or sitting upright; not during sleep
aggravating: Pain or the sight of blood

associated_symptoms.text: Lightheadedness or dizziness before the event
Brief jerking movements of the arms or legs during the faint
Feeling tired or confused for a short time afterward

pertinent_negatives: Chest pain or palpitations before the event
Loss of consciousness during exercise or while lying down
Confusion lasting more than a few minutes after waking
Loss of bladder or bowel control

argues_against: Fainting during exercise suggests a heart rhythm or structural heart cause

positives.text: Brief jerking movements during the faint
Feeling warm or sweaty before the event
Anxiety or emotional stress before the event

negatives: Symptoms occurring only when observed by others

atypical.how_it_differs: Fainting is more often caused by heart rhythm problems, medication effects, or orthostatic drops in blood pressure; warning symptoms may be absent and injuries from falls are more common.
missing_classic_features: Obvious trigger such as heat or emotion

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may not describe warning symptoms and instead appear pale, limp, or briefly unresponsive, often after a fall, pain, or crying.
missing_classic_features: Ability to describe lightheadedness or vision changes

atypical.how_it_differs: Fainting can occur from pressure of the uterus on the large veins when lying flat, from low blood sugar, or from anemia; it is more likely in later pregnancy.

general.mild: Alert, fully oriented, no distress; normal between episodes
general.moderate: Pale and diaphoretic, looks unwell but fully alert and oriented
general.severe: Pale, clammy, anxious; may have injured themselves in the fall
general.critical: Altered mental status or persistent unresponsiveness; may have obvious trauma

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure and heart rate supine, then after standing for 1 and 3 minutes
findings.finding: Drop in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mm Hg or diastolic of at least 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing, often with a rise in heart rate

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face, conjunctivae, and palms
findings.finding: Pallor
Cool, clammy, sweaty skin

findings.maneuver: Screen cranial nerves, strength, sensation, and coordination
findings.finding: No focal neurologic deficit
Alert and fully oriented with normal attention

findings.maneuver: Inspect the tongue and oral mucosa
findings.finding: No tongue biting or oral laceration

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the scalp, face, and skull
findings.finding: No hematoma, laceration, or palpable skull deformity
No carotid bruit

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart in the sitting and supine positions
findings.finding: Normal S1 and S2 without murmur, gallop, or rub

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart, including with the patient standing and squatting
findings.finding: Systolic murmur that changes with position, suggesting structural heart disease such as aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse and auscultate the heart
findings.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm or bradycardia
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheeze
No tenderness, mass, or pulsatile mass

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam when gastrointestinal bleeding is suspected
findings.finding: No gross blood or melena

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the limbs and joints
findings.finding: No deformity, swelling, or focal tenderness from the fall

labs.caveat: Anemia can cause or worsen fainting; a normal hemoglobin does not exclude acute blood loss early.
Hypoglycemia is a key mimic of fainting; check a bedside glucose in anyone with altered mental status or diabetes.
Hyponatremia can cause lightheadedness and confusion that mimic fainting.
Low potassium from diuretics can trigger arrhythmias and fainting.
A high BUN with a high BUN/creatinine ratio suggests dehydration or low blood volume.
Order when chest pain, exertional fainting, or concern for myocardial ischemia; a normal troponin does not exclude arrhythmic syncope.
Elevated in heart failure or structural heart disease; not a routine syncope test.
Thyroid disease can contribute to palpitations, arrhythmia, or orthostasis.
Check in anyone who could be pregnant; a positive result changes imaging and medication choices and raises concern for ectopic pregnancy with rupture.
Only when adrenal insufficiency is suspected from hypotension, hyperpigmentation, or chronic steroid use.

findings.finding: Sinus rhythm
Atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter with a rapid or slow ventricular response
Sinus bradycardia
Ventricular tachycardia or other wide-complex tachycardia
Heart rate under 50 beats per minute
Heart rate over 150 beats per minute
Prolonged PR interval (first-degree AV block)
Progressively lengthening PR then a dropped QRS (second-degree AV block, Mobitz I)
Intermittent dropped QRS without PR lengthening (Mobitz II) or complete AV block
Widened QRS over 120 ms
Left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria
Prolonged QTc over 480 ms
Short QTc under 340 ms (short QT syndrome)
ST elevation or depression suggesting acute myocardial ischemia or infarction
T-wave inversion in precordial leads
Epsilon wave or T-wave inversion in V1 to V3 (arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy)
Brugada pattern with coved ST elevation in V1 to V2
Pacemaker spikes or an implanted defibrillator

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected structural heart disease, murmur, exertional fainting, or abnormal ECG

findings.text: Aortic stenosis with a thickened, restricted aortic valve
Left ventricular hypertrophy with asymmetric septal thickening (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy)
Right ventricular dilation with reduced function (arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy)
Intracardiac mass such as an atrial myxoma

imaging.preferred_when: Head trauma from the fall, focal neurologic findings, or persistent altered mental status

findings.text: Intracranial hemorrhage such as subdural or subarachnoid blood

imaging.study: MRI brain with and without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Focal neurologic deficits or suspected seizure or structural brain lesion

findings.text: Cortical or hippocampal signal change suggesting seizure

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pulmonary embolism with tachycardia, hypoxemia, or pleuritic chest pain

findings.text: Filling defect in the pulmonary arteries

imaging.preferred_when: Dyspnea, chest pain, or suspected cardiac or pulmonary cause

findings.text: Normal heart size and clear lungs

initial.why: First-line test for arrhythmia, conduction disease, ischemia, and channelopathy
Bedside glucose to exclude hypoglycemia as a mimic
Anemia or infection contributing to fainting
Electrolytes, renal function, and hydration status
Pregnancy status before imaging and medications
Concern for myocardial ischemia or infarction
initial.only_if: chest pain, exertional fainting, or ischemic ECG changes

initial.why: Structural heart disease, murmur, or exertional fainting
initial.only_if: suspected structural heart disease or abnormal ECG

initial.why: Head trauma from the fall or focal neurologic findings
initial.only_if: head injury, focal deficit, or persistent altered mental status

confirmatory.test: MRI brain with and without contrast
confirmatory.why: Evaluates for seizure or structural brain lesion when neurologic cause is suspected
confirmatory.only_if: focal neurologic deficits or suspected seizure

supporting.why: Thyroid dysfunction can cause palpitations or arrhythmia
Adrenal insufficiency when hypotension or hyperpigmentation is present
Pulmonary embolism can present with syncope and tachycardia
Assesses cardiac size and pulmonary causes
supporting.only_if: dyspnea, chest pain, or suspected cardiopulmonary cause

not_indicated.why: Not a routine syncope test; use only in a validated pulmonary embolism pathway
No role unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Reserved for suspected hypoxemia or acid-base disturbance
Only if meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage is suspected
Not routine for syncope without trauma or focal findings

not_indicated.test: MRI brain with and without contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine for syncope without neurologic findings
Not routine without features suggesting pulmonary embolism

decision_points: Check a bedside glucose in any patient with altered mental status or diabetes
Obtain an ECG in every patient with fainting
Pregnancy test before CT or medications in anyone who could be pregnant
Consider cardiac cause when fainting occurs during exertion, while supine, or with palpitations
Orthostatic vital signs guide volume and medication review

differential.name: Seizure
differential.why_considered: Both cause transient loss of consciousness with a fall and sometimes brief jerking movements.
differential.trigger: Tongue biting, prolonged confusion after the event, or a witnessed tonic-clonic phase

history: Aura before the event
Tongue biting, especially the side of the tongue
Loss of bladder or bowel control
Confusion or drowsiness lasting minutes to hours after the event
No clear trigger such as standing, heat, or emotion
exam: Persistent postictal confusion or focal neurologic deficit
Lateralizing signs such as weakness on one side
labs: Elevated creatine kinase after a generalized seizure
Prolactin may be elevated shortly after a generalized seizure
imaging: MRI brain may show cortical or hippocampal signal change
CT head if trauma or acute intracranial cause is suspected

differential.name: Hypoglycemia
differential.why_considered: Low blood sugar causes lightheadedness, sweating, confusion, and loss of consciousness.
differential.trigger: Diabetes, insulin or sulfonylurea use, or altered mental status that improves with glucose

history: Diabetes with insulin or sulfonylurea use
Missed meal or excessive exercise
Symptoms improve quickly with sugar or food
No clear positional or emotional trigger
labs: Low serum glucose with symptoms that resolve after correction

differential.name: Orthostatic hypotension
differential.why_considered: A drop in blood pressure on standing causes lightheadedness and fainting, often with a similar trigger.

history: Symptoms only when standing up
Use of blood pressure medications, diuretics, or alpha-blockers
Dehydration, vomiting, or diarrhea
Parkinson disease or autonomic dysfunction
exam: Drop in systolic blood pressure of at least 20 mm Hg or diastolic of at least 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing
Heart rate may rise or fail to rise depending on cause

differential.name: Cardiac arrhythmia
differential.why_considered: Abnormal heart rhythms can cause sudden loss of consciousness without warning.
differential.trigger: Fainting during exertion, while supine, or with palpitations

history: Palpitations just before fainting
Fainting during exercise or while lying down
Family history of sudden cardiac death
Known heart disease
labs: Electrolyte abnormalities such as low potassium or magnesium
Elevated troponin if ischemia is the trigger
ecg: Arrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, or bradyarrhythmia
Conduction disease such as Mobitz II or complete heart block
Prolonged QTc, Brugada pattern, or epsilon waves
imaging: Echocardiogram may show structural heart disease

differential.name: Structural heart disease
differential.why_considered: Valve disease or cardiomyopathy can limit blood flow and cause fainting, especially with exertion.
differential.trigger: Murmur, exertional fainting, or abnormal ECG

history: Fainting during exertion
Chest pain or shortness of breath with activity
Family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiomyopathy
exam: Systolic murmur that changes with position
Signs of heart failure such as crackles or elevated jugular venous pressure
imaging: Echocardiogram showing aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or reduced ejection fraction

differential.name: Pulmonary embolism
differential.why_considered: A large clot in the lungs can cause sudden fainting with low oxygen and fast heart rate.
differential.trigger: Tachycardia, hypoxemia, or pleuritic chest pain after immobility or surgery

history: Recent surgery, immobility, or long travel
Pleuritic chest pain
Shortness of breath
exam: Signs of deep vein thrombosis such as leg swelling
imaging: CT pulmonary angiogram showing filling defect in pulmonary arteries

differential.name: Transient ischemic attack or stroke
differential.why_considered: Reduced blood flow to part of the brain can cause brief loss of consciousness or focal symptoms.
differential.trigger: Focal neurologic symptoms such as weakness, numbness, or trouble speaking

history: Sudden weakness or numbness on one side
Trouble speaking or understanding
Vision loss in one eye
Symptoms not clearly positional or emotional
imaging: CT head may be normal early

differential.name: Psychogenic pseudosyncope
differential.why_considered: Episodes of apparent loss of consciousness without true cerebral hypoperfusion.

history: Episodes occur only when observed by others
Prolonged duration without injury
No trigger such as standing or emotion
History of anxiety or trauma
exam: Normal vital signs and examination during and between episodes
Eyes may be closed and resistant to opening during episodes

severity.mild: Brief episode with clear warning, quick full recovery, no injury, and normal vital signs and ECG
severity.moderate: Recurrent episodes or a fall with minor injury; vital signs or ECG may be mildly abnormal
severity.severe: Fainting during exertion or while supine, with palpitations, chest pain, or abnormal ECG suggesting a cardiac cause
severity.critical: Persistent loss of consciousness, severe hypotension, life-threatening arrhythmia, or major trauma from the fall

red_flags.finding: Fainting during exertion or while lying down
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a cardiac cause such as arrhythmia or structural heart disease

red_flags.finding: Palpitations or chest pain before the event
Family history of sudden cardiac death
Abnormal ECG such as prolonged QTc, Brugada pattern, or heart block
Persistent confusion or focal neurologic deficit
red_flags.meaning: Suggests seizure, stroke, or other neurologic cause

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or tachycardia after the event
red_flags.meaning: Possible volume loss, bleeding, or pulmonary embolism
Requires evaluation for fracture, head injury, or internal bleeding

complications.name: Injury from fall
clues: Pain, swelling, or deformity after the event
Head trauma or loss of consciousness with injury

special_populations.differences: More often caused by arrhythmia, medication effects, or orthostatic hypotension; warning symptoms may be absent and injuries from falls are more common.
Young children may not describe warning symptoms and instead appear pale, limp, or briefly unresponsive, often after a fall, pain, or crying.
Fainting can occur from pressure of the uterus on the large veins when lying flat, from low blood sugar, or from anemia; it is more likely in later pregnancy.

key_questions.question: What were you doing right before you passed out?
key_questions.looking_for: Standing for a long time, warm or crowded room, pain, the sight of blood, or emotional stress suggests reflex fainting; fainting during exercise or while lying down suggests a cardiac cause

key_questions.question: Did you have any warning before it happened, like dizziness, warmth, nausea, or your vision dimming?
key_questions.looking_for: A brief warning of lightheadedness, warmth, sweating, or tunnel vision suggests reflex fainting; no warning suggests arrhythmia

key_questions.question: How long were you out, and how long until you felt normal again?
key_questions.looking_for: Seconds to about a minute of unconsciousness with full recovery within minutes; prolonged confusion suggests seizure

key_questions.question: Did anyone see jerking or shaking of your arms or legs?
key_questions.looking_for: Brief jerking can happen with fainting; a sustained tonic-clonic phase suggests seizure

key_questions.question: Did you bite your tongue, or lose control of your bladder or bowels?
key_questions.looking_for: Tongue biting or incontinence points toward seizure

key_questions.question: Did you have chest pain, palpitations, or a racing heart before or during the event?
key_questions.looking_for: Palpitations or chest pain suggest arrhythmia or ischemia

key_questions.question: Have you fainted before, and how many times?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent episodes raise concern and suggest a chronic cause

key_questions.question: Do you get lightheaded when you stand up quickly?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms only on standing suggest orthostatic hypotension

key_questions.question: Have you been drinking enough fluids? Any vomiting, diarrhea, or missed meals?
key_questions.looking_for: Dehydration or low blood sugar as a trigger

key_questions.question: What medicines do you take, including anything for blood pressure, water pills, or diabetes medicines?
key_questions.looking_for: Diuretics, antihypertensives, alpha-blockers, nitrates, or insulin can cause fainting

key_questions.question: Do you have any heart conditions, diabetes, or Parkinson disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Heart disease, diabetes, or autonomic dysfunction raises the risk of a dangerous cause

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family fainted or died suddenly at a young age?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of sudden cardiac death suggests an inherited arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy

key_questions.question: Did you hit your head or injure yourself when you fell?
key_questions.looking_for: Head trauma or other injury from the fall that needs evaluation

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes the workup and raises concern for ectopic pregnancy or anemia

key_questions.question: Any weakness or numbness on one side, trouble speaking, or a severe headache?
key_questions.looking_for: Focal neurologic symptoms suggest stroke or another neurologic cause

reasoning_points: A brief loss of consciousness with loss of muscle tone and quick, complete recovery
A warning of lightheadedness, warmth, sweating, or vision changes before the event
A trigger such as prolonged standing, a warm crowded room, pain, or emotional stress
No chest pain, no fainting during exertion, and no fainting while lying down
No tongue biting, incontinence, or prolonged confusion after the event
Orthostatic vital signs and a normal ECG
Bedside glucose checked to exclude hypoglycemia
Pregnancy considered in anyone who could be pregnant
Red flags for a cardiac cause reviewed, including exertional fainting, palpitations, abnormal ECG, and family history of sudden cardiac death

easy: Teenager or young adult who faints while standing in a warm, crowded room
Clear warning of lightheadedness, nausea, and tunnel vision
Quick full recovery with no injury
Normal exam, orthostatic vitals, and ECG
medium: Older adult on a diuretic with a drop in blood pressure on standing
Fainting with brief jerking movements that raises concern for seizure
Recurrent episodes with no obvious trigger
Mildly abnormal ECG that needs interpretation
hard: Fainting during exercise or while lying down suggesting a cardiac cause
Fainting with palpitations and a family history of sudden cardiac death
Older adult with no warning symptoms and a fall with injury
Young child who appears pale and limp after a fall or crying
Pregnant patient who faints when lying flat
